title: Do People Who Die by Suicide Go to Heaven?
excerpt: For centuries the church taught that suicide shut the door of heaven. Scripture never said so, and salvation has always rested on Christ rather than on the manner of a death.
body:
A mother is folding her son's shirts into a box, three weeks after the funeral, and she can't stop hearing something a cousin said in the parking lot of the funeral home. The cousin meant it gently. She said that when they were girls the church taught that people who did what he did could not go to heaven, but surely nobody believes that anymore. The mother has not slept well since. A man whose brother died the same way asked his pastor the question outright, and the pastor looked at the floor and said that was in God's hands, which was true, and which the man heard as a door closing. And somewhere tonight a teenager is typing the same question into a phone at two in the morning, and the person the teenager is asking about is not someone else.

Before anything else, a plain word to that last reader. If you're thinking about ending your life, stop reading and call or text 988 now. You can also use [Find Help](/help), which puts the crisis lines first. The page for the person who feels [empty and doesn't know why](/help/empty) says it in one line, and I'll repeat it here because it is true: "It can change." This essay will still be here tomorrow. You need a voice on the phone tonight more than you need an argument.

For everyone else, the question deserves a full answer, because a half answer has done real harm. The skeptic has watched the church handle this subject and has a fair complaint. A religion that claims to comfort the grieving, he says, took families at the worst moment of their lives and added the fear of hell to it. And it did so, he suspects, partly to frighten the living away from the same act. Some of that charge is true, and the church should hear it before it says anything else.

## Where the Old Teaching Came From

The belief that suicide damned did not come from nowhere, and the people who held it were not monsters. It grew from convictions that Christians still hold, and it is worth seeing those convictions clearly before seeing where they went wrong.

The first conviction is that a human life belongs to God before it belongs to anyone else. "You shall not murder" (Exodus 20:13) was read by the church as covering one's own life as well as a neighbor's. Paul told the Corinthians, "You are not your own, for you were bought with a price" (1 Corinthians 6:19-20), and while he was speaking about the body and sexual sin, the principle reached further: we are stewards of our lives, not owners of them. Augustine, writing *The City of God* in the years after Rome was sacked in 410, argued that a Christian may not take his own life even to escape the violence and shame of that catastrophe. Eight centuries later Thomas Aquinas gave three reasons the act was wrong: it goes against the natural love every creature has for its own life, it wounds the community the person belongs to, and it takes into human hands a gift that only God gives and only God may take back. Those arguments still carry weight. Most Christian traditions today would affirm all three.

The second conviction is that sin must be repented of, and here the reasoning took a fateful turn. If murder is a grave sin, and if a person dies in the very act of committing it, then the person seems to have died with no time to repent. On that logic suicide was not only a sin but a uniquely final one, the one sin a person could not take to confession. Add to this the conviction, common in the medieval church, that some sins sever a person from grace until they are confessed, and the conclusion followed with terrible simplicity.

The customs followed the conclusion. For centuries in much of Europe, those who died by their own hand were refused burial in consecrated ground, and in England they were buried outside the churchyard until the early nineteenth century. The Catholic Church's 1917 code of canon law still denied church funerals to people who had deliberately killed themselves. Families buried their dead in shame, or lied about how they died so they could bury them at all.

It should be said plainly that the church was trying to protect something precious. A tradition that treats every life as God's gift will want to say loudly that no life is disposable, including one's own, and there is mercy in a teaching that tells a desperate person that their life is not theirs to throw away. Many Christians who held the old view believed the fear of judgment might keep someone alive. Sometimes it may have. The Study Bible's note on [1 Samuel 31](/study/bible/1-samuel/31), the chapter where King Saul falls on his own sword, keeps that much of the tradition: the Bible "never presents taking one's own life as a good or honorable way out." Nothing in this essay takes that back.

## What Scripture Says, and What It Does Not

The Bible records a handful of these deaths, and it tells them with a restraint that is easy to miss. The same note lists them, "Abimelech in Judges 9, Saul and his armor-bearer here, Ahithophel in 2 Samuel 17, Zimri in 1 Kings 16, and Judas in Matthew 27," and observes that "in each case" Scripture "reports the act without extended comment." It never pronounces on anyone's eternal state. When Saul died, the men of Jabesh-gilead marched through the night to recover his body and bury it with honor (1 Samuel 31:11-13), and David, the man Saul had hunted for years, wrote him a lament (2 Samuel 1:17-27). The narrator treats him, in the note's words, "with sorrow rather than contempt."

Even Judas, whose death has been preached as a warning for centuries, is not used by Matthew to settle the question for anyone else. The note on [Matthew 27](/study/bible/matthew/27) says so directly: "Matthew tells what Judas did, and he does not pronounce on the fate of others who despair." It adds a line every grieving family should hear: "Despair told Judas there was no way back, and Peter's story in the same pages shows that despair lies." Peter denied Jesus three times on the same night Judas betrayed him. One man believed there was no way home, and the other was met on a beach after the resurrection and asked whether he loved his Lord.

Scripture also keeps the prayers of faithful people who wanted to die. Elijah sat under a broom tree and asked, "It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life, for I am no better than my fathers" (1 Kings 19:4). Job cursed his birth: "Let the day perish on which I was born" (Job 3:3). Paul told the Corinthians that in Asia "we were so utterly burdened beyond our strength that we despaired of life itself" (2 Corinthians 1:8). None of them is rebuked for the wish. God fed Elijah and let him sleep before he said a word to him about his calling. A desire to die is not, in Scripture, a sign that a person has stopped belonging to God.

And Scripture never names suicide as a sin beyond forgiveness. The one sin Jesus calls unforgivable is blasphemy against the Holy Spirit (Mark 3:28-29), which in its setting was the settled refusal of religious leaders to see the work of God in front of them and their decision to call it the work of Satan. In the same breath Jesus said, "all sins will be forgiven the children of man" (Mark 3:28). The site's page on [grief](/help/grief) puts the conclusion carefully, and I'd rather quote it than improve on it: "If you were told that someone who dies by suicide is lost forever, you were told more than anyone can know."

## What Salvation Rests On

The old teaching rested on a premise about the last moment of a life: that a person's eternal state depends on whether their final act was repented of. That premise deserves a hard look, because if it were true, it would condemn far more people than those who die by suicide.

No one dies with every sin confessed. The man who dies in a car accident on the way home from a bitter argument with his wife did not repent of his last words. The woman whose final thought before a stroke was resentment did not confess it. If salvation depended on a clean final ledger, none of us could be sure of anything. The gospel says something else. "For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast" (Ephesians 2:8-9). Salvation rests on what Christ has done, not on the timing of our last confession. "There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus" (Romans 8:1).

Paul ends that chapter with a list of everything that might seem able to cut a person off from God, and the list is deliberately total: "For I am sure that neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord" (Romans 8:38-39). The note on [Romans 8](/study/bible/romans/8) describes the chapter as framed by "no condemnation" at its opening and "no separation" at its close. Death is the first item on Paul's list. He did not add an exception for the manner of it.

The church has also learned something it did not always know about the minds of people who take their own lives. Much of the despair that ends in suicide is entangled with illness, with depression and anguish and pain that bend a person's perception until the lie that there is no way out feels like plain fact. The Catholic Church, which still calls the act gravely contrary to the love of God and neighbor, now teaches in its Catechism that serious psychological disturbance, anguish, or grave fear of suffering can diminish a person's responsibility. It goes on to say that the church should not despair of the eternal salvation of those who have taken their own lives, that God can provide an opportunity for repentance by ways known to him alone, and that the church prays for them. The 1983 revision of its canon law dropped the old refusal of funerals. Most Protestant churches arrived at a similar place by a different road: since salvation rests on Christ and not on the manner of a person's death, a believer's final act does not undo what God has done.

So where does that leave the mother with the box of shirts? It leaves her where Abraham stood when he argued with God over Sodom: "Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?" (Genesis 18:25). No pastor, no cousin, and no essay can pronounce on the eternal state of the one she lost, and the honest answer refuses to pretend otherwise in either direction. But she does not have to carry the old certainty that the door was shut. Scripture never told her that. The one who judges is the same one who wept at a friend's grave (John 11:35), and whose final word to his people is a love that nothing in all creation can break.

## What We Did

The church owes the grieving more than a corrected doctrine. It owes them an admission. We refused funerals to people whose families most needed one. We buried sons and daughters at the edge of the cemetery and let their parents carry that shame for the rest of their lives. We preached about suicide in ways designed to frighten, and some of the people sitting in the pews were already frightened enough. When the old teaching softened, many of us simply stopped talking about the subject, and the silence was its own kind of cruelty, because grieving families took it to mean the old judgment still stood and no one wanted to say so.

I'm a pastor, and pastors are trained to have a word ready. With this question the word often comes too fast, or doesn't come at all. The man whose pastor looked at the floor deserved better than a true sentence spoken like a closed door. He deserved someone to sit with him and say what Scripture actually says, and then to stay.

The grief page has advice for anyone who wants to help a family after a suicide, and it is worth repeating because the church has often done the opposite: "If the death was by suicide, don't ask how it happened, don't guess at why, and never suggest the person is at peace now." That last line matters as much as the first two. In our eagerness to undo the old cruelty, we can swing to a new one, speaking of the death as a release or a rest, which can sound to a struggling person like a recommendation. Scripture calls death "the last enemy" (1 Corinthians 15:26). It is never the cure.

## For the Family

If you lost someone this way, you are probably carrying more than grief. Many families carry guilt: the call not returned, the warning sign seen too late or not at all, the argument the week before. The grief page speaks to that, and its words are worth reading slowly: "If the death was by suicide, know that suicide rarely comes from any one thing and is not a measure of your love." You will likely never know everything that was happening inside the one you lost. Some of what you feel guilty about may be real, and real wrongs can be confessed and forgiven like any others. Much of it is love looking for a way it could have done more.

You may also carry anger, at them, at yourself, at God. Bring it to him. The psalms do. Psalm 88 ends without resolution, on the line "my companions have become darkness" (Psalm 88:18), and God kept that prayer in his book.

This kind of grief often needs more help than friends and a pastor can give. The page says it plainly: "A death by suicide, the death of a child, or a sudden or violent death more often needs skilled help." It also says this: "A support group for people who lost someone the same way can help as friends can't." Ask a hospice, a hospital chaplain, or a pastor where one meets. Seeing a counselor is not a failure of faith. This essay is not medical or psychological advice, and it cannot stand in for the people who can know you.

## If It Is You

Some readers came to this page because the question is about themselves. You may be wondering whether God would forgive you, or whether it would be so terrible, or whether the people around you would be better off. I want to answer you as plainly as I know how.

Please call or text 988 now, or call 911 if you're in danger. [Find Help](/help) has other lines. You don't have to explain yourself well to the person who answers. You can say, "I'm thinking about ending my life," and they will know what to do next.

The thoughts you are having are not a ruling on your worth or on your faith. Elijah, Job and Paul all reached the end of themselves, and God did not leave any of them there. The voice that tells you there is no way back is the same voice that spoke to Judas, and Peter's story shows it was lying. When Paul wrote to the Philippians from prison, uncertain whether he would live or die, he admitted that part of him longed to depart and be with Christ, and then he chose otherwise for the sake of the people who needed him: "to remain in the flesh is more necessary on your account" (Philippians 1:24). The people around you are not better off without you. They need you to remain.

Moses set the choice before Israel in words that still stand: "I have set before you life and death, blessing and curse. Therefore choose life" (Deuteronomy 30:19). Choosing life tonight may look very small. It may mean making one phone call, telling one person the truth, putting distance between yourself and whatever you were thinking of using, and letting someone sit with you until morning. That small choice is enough for tonight.

## The Judge of All the Earth

The cousin in the parking lot was right that few churches teach the old doctrine now, but she was wrong to think that settled it. The mother does not need to hear that a teaching has gone out of fashion. She needs to hear why it was never the whole truth, and what is true instead.

What is true is that her son's life was a gift from God and that its ending was a grief to God. What is true is that no one can see into the last hour of another person's mind, and that the God who can see it is the one who gave his own Son for sinners. What is true is that the manner of a death is not the measure of a soul, and that salvation has always rested on Christ and never on a clean final page. And what is true is that death, however it comes, is an enemy Christ has promised to destroy, not a door anyone should open early.

She will not get every answer she wants this side of the resurrection. But she can fold the shirts, and grieve, and leave her son with the Judge of all the earth, who wept at Lazarus's tomb though he was about to raise him, and who has promised that he "will wipe away every tear from their eyes" (Revelation 21:4).

*"The LORD is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit."* (Psalm 34:18)

*"Nor height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord."* (Romans 8:39)
